newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais asks staff to approve pay cut.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais asks staff to approve pay cut.

text.p: Troubled state-controlled French bank Credit Lyonnais will write to its workers next month asking them to accept a pay cut as part of an agreement to save 1,100 jobs, a spokesman said on Monday.

The so-called "solidarity contribution" amounting to 0.6 percent of employees' gross annual wages was part of a deal in December with unions aimed at salvaging some of the 5,000 bank jobs due to be axed. "We will be writing to all the personnel telling them what is planned," said a bank spokesman.
It is one of the first times such a large enterprise in France has tested the "solidarity" of its employees on a company-wide basis in such a fashion.
The job-cutting programme is part of the bank's struggle to improve profitability and ready itself for privatisation.
The bank, which has 34,700 employees in France, had losses of 21 billion francs ($4 billion) between 1992 and 1994 from a disastrous expansion spree before edging back into profit last year.
The bank has been rescued twice by the state and it is expected to be bailed out a third time in 1997 to boost its solvency ratios to prepare it for sale.
Under the three-year job-saving agreement, the working hours of 7,000 workers will be cut to 33 hours from 39. They will work a four-day week.
The pay cut is part of a package of measures to cushion the impact of the reduction in working hours on wages with the greatest help coming from the new Robien law.

Named after its framer, Gilles de Robien, a member of the ruling centre-right coalition government, the law allows a substantial reduction in employer social security contributions to prevent layoffs or create jobs.
The measures mean the short-time Credit Lyonnais workers will be paid for a 37-and-one-quarter hour week and will lose only five percent of their pay.

Although some of the bank's unions opposed the agreement, a Credit Lyonnais spokesman said the bank was confident workers would agree to the pay cut which amounts to an average of less than 100 francs per employee.
The bank now will cut 4,046 jobs between now and 1998, but it is hoping to avoid compulsory redundancies by using such measures as early retirement.

Financial analysts have said the bank must trim staff to find a buyer. In November, U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs, advisor to the French government, was reported to have been told by potential purchasers of Credit Lyonnais they would only look at it if they had a free hand to cut jobs.
The government has said it wants to privatise Credit Lyonnais as soon as possible but the bank has said it is unlikely to be in a fit state to be sold until mid-1998.
The bank, which had pledged to submit its privatisation plan to the government before year end, is believed to have done so but has declined to confirm it officially.
-- Penny MacRae, Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452 ($ = 5.241 French Francs)
